description: Last year, we were unfortunate to lose. But this year, WE want to win.
summary: The MODIS and VIIRS Burning Activity Calendar (MaVBAC) is a web app that turns more than 20 years of NASA satellite fire detections into one consistent, easy-to-read history for any area on Earth. Satellites have tracked active fires since 2000, but the record is split between the older MODIS sensors and the newer, sharper VIIRS sensors, whose counts can’t be compared directly. Our app harmonizes the two into a single time series. Users draw an area on the map and choose a date range. They then see a calendar of fire activity by month and year, real fire detections on a 3D map, and how the current month compares with the historical median. Every view is downloadable as a CSV. The app doesn’t predict individual fires. Instead, it shows emergency managers, land managers and scientists when fire season peaks, which years were unusually active, and whether conditions right now are above normal. That helps them plan staffing, monitor sensitive regions, and respond earlier.
details:
MaVBAC: Is Your Town in Fire Season Right Now?

Most people find out when they smell the smoke. Wildfire seasons are getting longer and less predictable, but the satellite record that could warn us is hard to read. When NASA moved from the MODIS instrument to VIIRS, fire counts jumped overnight because of the sensor change, not because of real fires. Anyone comparing "this year vs. the past" was really comparing two different instruments.

What is MaVBAC?

MaVBAC, the MODIS and VIIRS Burning Activity Calendar, is a fire-history platform that answers two questions for any place on Earth: when does this land burn, and how likely is a wildfire there in the next 30 days? It turns raw satellite detections into a record you can trust, then turns that record into a warning that indicates when there could be a potential wildfire and where it could be.

One Ecosystem, Three Ways In

MaVBAC is three connected parts that share one live server, the same NASA data and the same forecast:

  • The MaVBAC website is primarily for analysis: the harmonized calendar, the fire map, the 3D view and the Wildfire Outlook.
  • The Fire Connect page is the live message board for first-responders and operators, on the web.
  • The Fire Connect app is the same board as an app that installs on any iPhone or Android home screen in seconds, with no app store. Here, civilians can send immediate messages which the operators and first-responders will see.

Information flows between all three. A fire reported from a phone appears on the website's board within seconds, tagged with our 30-day forecast and the live weather at that spot. An official alert from a verified forecaster or responder reaches every screen at once. The calendar and forecast that analysts study on the website are the same ones that give context to every report. Data, forecast and communication live in one place, so knowing the risk and acting on it happen together.

From Raw Detections to a Record You Can Trust

MaVBAC learns a month-by-month VIIRS-to-MODIS ratio on a 1° grid from 2012–2018, then tests it on data from 2019 onward, years it never saw. Error on those test years is 5.7% in Australia, 15% in Mato Grosso (Brazil) and 17% in Northern California. Pick any area and date range and you get a year-by-month calendar of burning activity in three views. The Harmonized view puts the whole record on one scale, the Raw view shows the fake sensor jump, and the Anomaly view compares each month with its usual level.

A Forecast That Shows Its Work

For California, Australia, Brazil, Africa and the whole world, we trained gradient-boosted models on NASA FIRMS detections, past weather and season. They predict whether satellites will see fire in each square over the next 30 days. On 2023 to now, years held out from training, the model beat a "same month in past years" baseline in every region; in California, PR-AUC rose from 0.40 to 0.50. The Wildfire Outlook turns this into a verdict and lists its reasons: how often wildfires started nearby at this time of year, whether people or lightning usually start them, the local fire season, the long-term climate, and whether this week is hotter, drier or windier than normal.

Real Wildfires, Not Just Hot Pixels

Satellites also see farm burning and planned (prescribed) burns. In the USA, MaVBAC cross-checks against national wildfire incident records, so the verdict is about real wildfires. That includes the ones people start, like yard-debris burning, equipment sparks and arson.

See It in 3D, Then Talk About It

The map shows live FIRMS fire detections, a 30-day fire-likelihood layer, and a 3D view that switches to Google Photorealistic 3D when you zoom in to a city. In Fire Connect, the public posts fire reports with a location, and verified forecasters and responders post official alerts. Fire Connect always reminds people to call their emergency number first.

Where We Go Next

Detailed coverage now spans California, Australia, Brazil and Africa, chosen for their frequent, large fires. With bigger servers, we will extend it to the whole planet, so anyone, anywhere, can know their fire season before the smoke arrives.
